Mapping stated: 'the Gabor filter is used to represent the retinal processing mechanism of the spike train' (Discussion) and the RF property matrix is integrated into the loss ('we implemented a method that integrated receptive field property matrix into loss function', Abstract); the artifact runs end-to-end on real spike trains, but the brain-level correspondence (Gabor-AE as visual processing) is engineering analogy.

Table 1 compares the proposed Gabor-AE + RF-weighted loss against auto-encoder baselines (MSE loss: SSIM 0.7281; SSIM loss: 0.8088; proposed: 0.8174; PSNR 14.89 vs 14.64) - a comparison exists, but gains are marginal and the two brain-inspired components (Gabor filters, RF weighting) are introduced together without individual ablation, so attribution to the correspondence is not isolated.

Two real neural datasets (macaque V1 and salamander RGC spike trains, gratings plus scene data), i.e. cross-species and cross-region - but stimuli are simple (4 orientations) and the paper concedes 'its performance is still poor for stimuli from complex visual images'.

Abstract's claim ('our method can effectively combine receptive field features to reconstruct images, providing a new approach') is matched by the two-dataset demonstration and Table 1; no overclaim of state-of-the-art is made.

The pipeline premise is citation-based: LGN/thalamus pre-processing (Cudeiro & Sillito 2006; Derrington et al. 1984) and 'engram cells... only activate for specific stimuli' (Xie et al. 2014; Tonegawa et al. 2015; Quiroga et al. 2005) in Sec 1; the inference to 'internal generative models for different kinds of concepts in the human brain' is explicitly speculative ('suggest there could be').
note: Sparse coding in V1 (Olshausen & Field 1996) and engram activation studies (Liu et al. 2012) are the canonical supports but were not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: Mapping stated (Fig. 1, Sec 2): the denoiser 'similar to what LGN does' and per-category autoencoders 'can be regarded as internal models for specific concepts' mimicking sparse engram coding - the components are implemented and function, but the correspondence to thalamus/engram circuits is design analogy, not verified.

Sec 4: comparison against SOTA defenses (adversarial training, ABS/biABS) plus CNN/biCNN baselines across 42 foolbox attacks (Table 1, 'biDIM still beats the SOTA on the overall robustness'), with an ablation study (Table 2) covering the denoiser (IM without denoiser) and the internal-model structure (single-IM vs DIM).
note: Clean accuracy is lower than baselines (96% vs 99%), acknowledged by the authors.

justification_quote: Robustness is evaluated broadly over 42 attacks (L0/L1/L2/Linf, white- and black-box) - but only on MNIST with simple networks; no other dataset or task.

Abstract's claims ('evaluate DIM over 42 adversarial attacks... effectively defenses against all the attacks and outperforms the SOTA on the overall robustness') match Table 1; the abstract omits that evaluation is MNIST-only and that clean accuracy trails baselines (96% vs 99%, Sec 4).

The temporal-coding premise is citation-plus-belief: 'in temporal-encoding, the precise time duration required to spike is believed to encode the neuron output information' (Sec I, citing [5]); no own biological evidence, and rate-vs-temporal coding remains debated.

Mapping is device-physics level and verified in co-simulation: the neuron activation function 'is obtained from stochastic-LLG simulations of the superparamagnetic MTJ device' calibrated to experimental measurements (Sec IV), and 'the accuracy of the hardware network approaches the ideal baseline software accuracy with only a 2/3-spike confidence' (Fig. 3c) - the MTJ network is shown to instantiate the computation.
note: Device-level simulation calibrated to measurement; no full-chip demonstration.

justification_quote: Controlled comparisons: test accuracy 97.41% 'at par with iso-architecture standard deterministic networks' (ReLU network 97.03%) and sparsity benchmarked 'against an iso-accuracy rate-encoded stochastic MTJ network' showing '1.6x reduction in spiking sparsity for the hidden layer and 3.77x... for the output layer' (Sec IV) - the sparsity gain is attributed to temporal encoding by matched comparison.
note: Single dataset (MNIST); co-simulation only.

justification_quote: Two architectures (784x10 and 784x400x10) behave consistently, but everything is MNIST; 'Scaling to deeper architectures is expected to improve the sparsity and latency benefits' is explicit extrapolation beyond the demonstrated setting.

Abstract's quantitative claim ('Hardware-algorithm co-design analysis demonstrates 97.41% accuracy of a state-compressed 3-layer spintronics enabled stochastic spiking network on the MNIST dataset with high spiking sparsity') matches Sec IV exactly, and 'analysis' honestly denotes co-simulation rather than hardware measurement.

The inspiration is explicitly speculative: 'the possible influence of quantum effects on biological processes and the related quantum brain hypothesis have been theoretically investigated (Vaziri and Plenio, 2010; Fisher, 2015...)' (Sec: quantum-inspired SNN) - no evidence, in this paper or verified literature, that brain coding uses quantum superposition.
note: The complex (rate+phase) spike representation motivation is also asserted, not evidenced.

justification_quote: The superposition-to-spike mapping is formalized and implemented: complementary original/inverted images 'encoded as a superposition state' (Eq. 5) transferred to spike trains with phase estimation (Eqs. 10, 16-19), processed by two-compartment SNN neurons - the computation is instantiated under a stated formal mapping, but the anchor to biological brain phenomena is metaphorical.

Controlled comparison on the same superposition-encoded inputs: FC ANN, CNN, VGG16, ResNet101, DenseNet121 'all models are trained with original image and then tested on the background reverse image' and fail, while 'QS-SNN... retained the same accuracy as when classifying the original data' (Results); robustness further tested under reverse pixel noise and AWGN (Figs. 5-6).
note: Inversion invariance is partly built into the input encoding (the mirror image is included in the superposition by construction).

justification_quote: Two datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST) under inversion, reverse-pixel and Gaussian noise - all within image classification robustness; no other task family or modality.

Abstract's claims ('can handle reversal of image background color', 'more robust performance compared with traditional ANN models, especially when processing noisy inputs') match the Results on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST vs the named ANN/CNN baselines; closing claim is hedged ('will inform future efforts').

The premise is philosophical framing with citations: 'One influential view in theoretical neuroscience sees the brain as a function-computing device' ([2], Sec I) and memristors as synapse models ([9]) - no own biological evidence.
note: Memristor-as-synapse literature (e.g. Jo et al. 2010) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: The instantiation is tested directly: mPES drives simulated Nb-doped SrTiO3 memristive devices (device model fitted to experimental data, with pulse-count stochasticity and device-to-device variation, Sec II) to implement five functions, compared against PES on ideal linear synapses and the analytic NEF gold standard - 'mPES was able to modulate the memristive synapses' resistances which, when translated to network weights, implemented f as well or better than PES' (Sec III).
note: Simulation of device physics calibrated to measurement; no hardware chip.

justification_quote: The abstract's claim is parity, and it is tested by controlled comparison: mPES vs PES vs NEF over ten runs per function with interleaved 2.5s learning/testing blocks (Figs. 3-4, Table I final-block errors within PES confidence intervals; faster learning on circular convolutions).
note: No performance gain over ideal synapses is claimed; efficiency benefits are prospected, not measured.

justification_quote: Five functions of varying dimensionality (multiplications, 2-D and 3-D circular convolution) within the Nengo function-approximation benchmark - one framework, one task family, simulated devices only.

Abstract's claim ('we show that we are able to at least match the performance obtained when using ideal, linear synapses') matches the Sec III parity results; the efficiency framing is prospective ('to move towards more efficient, brain-inspired computing').

The E/I-balance premise is citation-based: balance 'crucial for optimal brain function [10]', disruptions linked to anesthesia/epilepsy [11]-[13], and the adaptation rule 'inspired by activity homeostasis in neurobiology [18-22]' (Sec I) - no own biological evidence.
note: Canonical E/I-balance literature (van Vreeswijk & Sompolinsky 1996; Okun & Lampl 2008) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: Mapping stated: 4:1 excitatory/inhibitory ratio and 1:4 strength ratio 'consistent with their approximate relative proportions in the brain [17]', Dale's law connectivity, and a local inhibitory adaptation rule targeting firing rates (Sec II-III); the mechanisms are implemented, and the paper honestly reports that the Dale's-law restriction 'does not improve or impair RC performance; shuffling the connections yields similar results' (Supp. Fig. 3) - one correspondence element tested and found inert.

Controlled comparison isolating the adaptation: Fig. 3B contrasts 'the best non-adaptive reservoir (gray; optimized via beta and theta)' with adaptive reservoirs (homogeneous and heterogeneous target rates) across 100 runs and four tasks; abstract's 'improving performance by up to 130%... compared with globally tuned RCs'; adaptation also corrects local imbalances in already-balanced reservoirs (Fig. 2B).
note: 'Up to 130%' is a best-case figure.

justification_quote: Four tasks spanning linear (memory capacity) and nonlinear prediction (NARMA-10, Mackey-Glass, Lorenz), with heterogeneous rates giving task-general performance without per-task tuning (Fig. 3) - but all within the reservoir-computing paradigm; no other domain.

Abstract's claims match the evidence: best performance 'in balanced or slightly over-inhibited regimes' (Fig. 1C-D), 'up to 130%' improvement hedged as best case, heterogeneity claim matching Fig. 3B; brain-level claims are framed as inspiration ('demonstrating how brain-inspired mechanisms can improve RC performance').

The cognitive premise is citation-based: humans perceive the whole ('forest') before details ('trees'), 'originally observed and experimentally documented by cognitive psychologist David Navon [20, 21]', and dual-channel LSF/HSF processing 'in human vision [42-45]' (Sec 1) - no own biological evidence.
note: Navon 1977 (Cognitive Psychology 9:353-383) is canonical but was not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: Mapping stated: 'a dual-channel design that mimics the complementary low spatial frequency (LSF) and high spatial frequency (HSF) processing in human vision', with the classical pathway 'simulating the EVC and OFC' and the quantum pathway analyzing HSF patches (Sec 2, Fig. 1a) - components are implemented and ablated (Fig. 4), but the brain correspondence is design analogy.

Fig. 2: BIQC vs classical baselines (MLP, CNN, SWinT, XGBoost) and quantum/hybrid baselines (WeiNet, QC-Inception, QNN, RealAmplitudes, ExplicitVQC, DynamicQNN) across four datasets, 'outperforming the top baseline (CNN) by a significant margin of 8.42% in accuracy' on DTD; Fig. 4 ablations remove EVC module, OFC attention, and the HSF pathway, validating each component.
note: All results are numerical simulations (PennyLane); tasks are binary classifications.

justification_quote: Four datasets spanning digits, natural scenes, medical and texture images at varying resolutions, plus a universality test transferring the Guiding Paradigm to another architecture (QC-Inception, Fig. 3) - but all within image classification, in simulation.

Abstract's claim ('Numerical simulations on diverse datasets, including high-resolution images, show the BIQC's superior accuracy and scalability compared to existing methods') matches Fig. 2's benchmark comparisons and honestly labels the evidence as numerical simulation.

The pathway premise is citation-based: 'pathways between pMFC and anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) are involved in post-error attentional adaptation' [14]-[16] and depression dynamics in ACC/pMFC [14] (Sec 1, Fig. 1 caption) - no own biological evidence.

Mapping stated: the model 'integrates an IANN and a VAE by mimicking the emotional processing pathways between pMFC and aMCC [16, 18, 21]', with gradient learning 'as a common neuromodulator' plus local associative memory (Sec 1, Sec 3); interpretive outputs (firing rates Fig. 6, PLV networks Fig. 7) are qualitatively 'reconcil[ed]' to clinical findings (prefrontal dysfunction etc.) - analogy plus qualitative consistency, no direct test.

Table 1 (MODMA): BIG 89.9% vs EEGNet 69.9%, TS-SEFFNet 74.7%, Deep ConvNet 76.2%, HEMAsNet 80.7% (P<1e-2); Table 2 (SEED): BIG 83.6% is mid-pack (below IAG 86.3% and BSNN 86.4%) - baseline comparisons exist, but the abstract's claimed ablations of the impulsive-attention module and hybrid learning are not present in the text body, so attribution to the brain-inspired components is unverified.

Two public EEG datasets with different sampling rates and label spaces (MODMA depression, SEED emotion) plus a few-shot pattern using generated EEG (Sec 4.2, Fig. 5b) - within EEG classification; no other modality or task family.

Abstract claims exceed the evidence in the text: 'classification accuracy above 89%' fails on SEED (83.6%, Table 2); 'reducing computational cost by nearly 11% over the baseline EEGNet' and 'Ablation studies justify the poised brain-inspired characteristic' have no corresponding section, table or figure in the body (only the classification Tables 1-2, ROC, few-shot and interpretation figures are present).
note: Possible text-layer loss cannot be excluded, but grades follow the pinned text layer.

justification_quote: The delay-learning premise rests on citation: 'Biological evidence shows that reward-related neurotransmitters can control the process of myelination and demyelination [23]' (Sec 2.1) and the role of synaptic delays in spatio-temporal learning [21] - no own biological evidence; the reward-myelination link is emerging literature.

Mapping stated with explicit equations: the reward-modulated delay learning (RDL) rule modifies synaptic delays with reward/punishment polarity (Sec 2.1), combined with R-STDP weights, UDL delays, homeostasis and decentralization mechanisms (Sec 3.2); the artifact demonstrably learns delay features (Figs. 4-6), but the correspondence to myelination biology is analogy.

Table 1 compares against deep, supervised-SNN and biologically-plausible-SNN models on DVS128-Gesture, and the Validation section runs disable-one-mechanism ablations (e.g. deactivating intervallic homeostasis causes 'a 0.5% and 2.1% decrease... on the train and test sets', Fig. 7) - component contributions are ablation-controlled.
note: The proposed model's own Table-1 accuracy is garbled in the text layer (*78.08 with a 98.24% note on three activities).

justification_quote: Single benchmark (DVS128-Gesture, with the 11th class excluded, Sec 3.1) and single task family; the Validation experiments vary mechanisms, not tasks, datasets or scales.

Abstract's claims are scoped to the benchmark ('we evaluate the performance of our model against other models using a benchmark dataset... DVS-128 Gesture. The results show that our model outperforms previous biologically plausible models and competes with deep supervised models') and match Table 1's ordering.

The cortical premise is citation-based: 'Cognitive neuroscience [7] shows that human multimodal cognition involves: (1) unimodal encoding... in primary sensory cortices; (2) direct neural pathways... (3) higher-order cortical regions' (Sec 1) and the Fig. 1 audiovisual-cortex analogy - no own biological evidence.
note: Multisensory-integration literature (e.g. Stein & Stanford 2008) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: Mapping stated: dual-stream unimodal spike encoders stand for sensory-specific cortices, 'Early alignment mimics direct neural pathways', and Spike Fusion stands for higher-order audiovisual integration producing soft supervisory labels (Sec 1, Fig. 1); components are implemented and ablated, but the cortical correspondence is design analogy.

Tables 1-2: 'outperforming all ANN baselines' on MSCOCO 1K and FLICKR 30K 1K (Recall@K), remaining 'highly competitive' on MSCOCO 5K; Table 4-5 ablations isolate Bidirectional Hard Alignment (R@Sum 511.3/506.9/523.9) and the Early-Alignment/Spike-Fusion components (511.6 dual-stream only); Table 3 gives theoretical energy (0.626 mJ, 78% lower than HREM).
note: Energy is a theoretical estimate following prior SNN practice, not measured hardware.

justification_quote: Two widely-used ITR benchmarks (Flickr30K, MSCOCO 1K/5K) - a single task family; no other multimodal task or modality pair.

Abstract's claims are largely matched: 'top-tier retrieval accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art ANN counterparts' holds on the 1K test sets and only partially on MSCOCO 5K ('surpasses several state-of-the-art methods on multiple metrics', Sec 4); 'exceptionally low energy consumption' is a theoretical estimate (Table 3).

The attention premise is citation-based: ARSLIF 'emulates the mechanism of retuning of cellular signal selectivity in the brain attention systems' (Abstract; Sec I: 'we take inspiration from an attention perceptual mechanism of the brain') - no own biological evidence for the structure->computation link.
note: Auditory-attention receptive-field retuning literature (e.g. Fritz et al. 2007) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: Mapping stated at neuron level: ARSLIF adapts firing-rate targets and activation thresholds (Table I parameters) to emulate selectivity retuning; the mechanism is implemented and trained, but its correspondence to cellular retuning in brain attention systems is analogy, not verified.

Controlled comparisons isolating the brain-inspired component and structure: Fig. 7 benchmarks ARSLIF against LIF, Sigmoid, Soft Threshold and Target-Freq LIF activation functions across pink/blue/purple noise levels ('the ARSLIF model consistently outperforms... particularly at the extremes of the noise spectrum'); Table IV ablates multi-head attention (MAE 9.1419) and Bi-LSTM (11.2401) vs full model (8.8310); Table VI shows DAIC-WOZ superiority over baselines.
note: AVEC2014 comparison vs SOTA is honestly mixed (lower RMSE, weaker MAE than [40][28][42]).

justification_quote: Three datasets (MODMA classification, AVEC2014 and DAIC-WOZ regression/detection) with synthetic-noise robustness sweeps - all within audio-based depression assessment; no other disorder or modality.

Abstract's claims are consistent with the evidence: state-of-the-art is claimed only for MODMA (0.8974 accuracy), and the AVEC2014/DAIC-WOZ claims are noise-robustness enhancements (Fig. 7) rather than SOTA accuracy - matching the mixed AVEC2014 comparison the paper itself reports.

external_citation_verified_route: web search (this session): Bi & Poo 1998, J Neurosci 18(24):10464-10472 - spike-timing-dependent synaptic modification in hippocampal neurons
justification_quote: The plasticity premise is citation-based: STDP listed among brain-inspired learning mechanisms with citations [10],[11] (Sec I); no own biological evidence.
note: The paper's own rule is a binary stochastic STDP variant - heavily abstracted from biology.

justification_quote: Hardware-level instantiation demonstrated: EON-1 implements IF neurons with a stochastic binary STDP rule (Algorithm 1, Sec III) including learning-threshold comparators and a learning engine running 'on-chip, in parallel with learning and inference' (Sec III-B); evaluated on FPGA (Xilinx VU37P, 100MHz) and gate-level post-synthesis ASIC simulation (GF-22nm, 500MHz) (Sec IV-A).
note: No fabricated ASIC; the binary 1-bit-weight STDP is an engineering abstraction of synaptic plasticity.

justification_quote: The headline utility claim is comparative: 'only 1% energy overhead for learning, by far the lowest overhead when compared to other SoTA solutions' with Table III benchmarking EON-1 (87.8-92.8% on downscaled 14x14 MNIST) against TCSI'21/TCSII'21/Neuro'17/ICTA'23 FPGA solutions, plus the face-detection/CIFAR10 UHD streaming task for online adaptation.
note: Accuracy is comparable-not-superior to some baselines (e.g. 95.49% for ICTA'23).

justification_quote: Three task settings (MNIST benchmark, binary face detection from pre-trained network, UHD real-time streaming) across FPGA and post-synthesis ASIC instantiations - but all small-scale edge feature-extraction tasks; no large-scale or other-domain evaluation.

Abstract's claims match the evaluation: the 1% learning energy overhead and 'comparable inference accuracy' correspond to the Sec IV comparisons, and the HD/UHD real-time claim to the streaming experiment; scope is a processor prototype (FPGA + ASIC simulation), which 'we report results' reflects.

Neurocognitive premises are citation-level analogies: tokens mapped 'to specialized nodes analogous to cortical areas' (with Broca's area [1] as example) and signal propagation 'simulates electrophysiological information dynamics observed in brain activity' (Abstract, Sec 2) - no own biological evidence and no established literature that token-to-node mapping mirrors cortical organization.

SiFu is implemented under a stated mapping (semantic nodes as cortical areas, signal-energy propagation with reset strategy, Sec 3-4, Figs. 1-4) and trains successfully at 1-2B scale - the instantiation is demonstrated as feasible, but the correspondence to electrophysiological brain dynamics is analogy.

No comparative evidence: the paper states 'SiFu's departure from representation learning further precludes direct comparisons to GPT-1's benchmarking or standard LLM fine-tuning metrics'; experiments 'validate two core properties... stable learning dynamics and functional sequence continuation' via training loss (Fig. 5) and Chinese/English completion case studies (Tables 4-5) - suggestive, no baselines, no ablations.
note: 'GPT-1-level generative capabilities' is asserted via case studies without metrics.

justification_quote: No evidence beyond the demonstrated setting: actual models are 1-2B parameters on ~100M Wikipedia tokens with a 4,000-token vocabulary and 32-token sequences; the 100-200B feasibility is parameter-count analysis ('Scalability analyses confirm the feasibility'), and emergent abilities are explicitly 'insufficient to demonstrate'.

Abstract claims exceed the evidence: 'multiple transformative breakthroughs: natural multi-modal compatibility... and the first global-scale simulation of brain-like information processing' are not demonstrated - experiments validate only stable learning and sequence continuation on single-modality text at 1-2B scale, with multimodality, interpretability-at-scale and 100-200B variants remaining design claims or analyses.

external_citation_verified_route: web search (this session): Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997, Science 275(5306):1593-1599 - dopamine neurons encode reward prediction error
justification_quote: The neurocognitive premises are citation-based: 'dopaminergic signals play a crucial role by encoding prediction errors' (Sec 1, Fig. 2), LLM as cerebral cortex, PFC-like memory gating and basal-ganglia winner-takes-all action selection - all carried by citation, no own biological evidence.
note: External verification covers the dopaminergic prediction-error part; the basal-ganglia/PFC analogies rest on the paper's citations, not independently verified.

justification_quote: Mapping stated module-by-module (Fig. 2): LLM 'simulates the cerebral cortex', dynamic memory module 'modelled after the prefrontal cortex' with PE-driven gating (Sec 3.2), and lightweight specialists emulating basal ganglia routed by 'a strict winner-takes-all mechanism' via Gumbel-Softmax (Sec 3.3) - implemented and ablated, but the brain correspondence is design analogy.

Tables 2-4: Macro-F1 78.97% (Kaggle) and 68.98% (Pandora), 'surpassing the previous state-of-the-art model TAE by 6.90% and 5.93%', across baselines including SVM/XGBoost/LSTM/Transformers and GPT-4o/DeepSeek-V3 (zero-shot and CoT); Table 5 ablation removes Working Memory and the PE Signal, confirming each component's contribution (Sec 4.3).
Two datasets (Kaggle MBTI, Pandora Reddit comments) with severe class imbalance (Table 1) - both personality detection from text; no other trait taxonomy, language domain or task.

Abstract's claim ('Extensive experiments on the Kaggle and Pandora datasets demonstrate that HIPPD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines') matches Tables 2-4, with the brain-level claims framed as emulation ('emulates the hierarchical information processing of the human brain').

Survey item: 'In this survey, we examine algorithms for conducting credit assignment in artificial neural networks that are inspired or motivated by neurobiology' (Abstract); the biological grounding of synaptic plasticity and credit assignment is synthesis over cited literature, not own evidence.
note: FLAG: review/survey paper; no own artifact or experiment; all transitions graded as citation-only evidence.

justification_quote: The survey organizes brain-inspired learning schemes into six families and describes their mechanisms (Sec 2-4), but these are third-party algorithms described with citations; no correspondence is instantiated or verified by this paper.

Claims about backprop alternatives are comparative-synthesis only ('consider these in the context of backpropagation of errors and its known criticisms'); the survey runs no experiments attributing performance to any correspondence.
No cross-task or cross-scale evaluation is performed; the survey maps the field's landscape and open problems.

The abstract's claim is the survey scope itself (taxonomy of six families, comparison to backprop criticisms, 'results of this review are meant to encourage future developments'), which the paper delivers; no experimental improvement is claimed.

The premise is a psychological hypothesis, cited: 'As hypothesized by Kahneman [19], the human brain operates using two distinct systems' with System 2 claimed to experience 'minimum forgetting' in humans (Sec 1) - assertion by citation to dual-process theory; no own biological evidence.
note: Dual-process (System 1/2) is a cognitive-psychology framework, and the System-2-forgetting-resistance claim is speculative, so no external verification.

justification_quote: Mapping stated: 'artificial neural networks are believed to behave very similarly to System 1, while symbolic reasoners share similar [properties to] System 2' (Sec 1); NeSyBiCL pairs a neural reasoner (fast adaptation) with a symbolic graph reasoner (retention) plus a knowledge-transfer mechanism (Sec 3-4) - implemented and run, but the correspondence to dual-process cognition is analogy.

Controlled comparisons with 4 repeats and standard deviations: fine-tuning (lower bound), multi-task (upper bound), EWC and ER baselines, and a pure-symbolic variant that ablates the neural reasoner (Sec 5.1), on two 10-task compositional benchmarks (Clevr, Sketch) using A_all and A_last metrics.
note: Benchmarks are introduced by the authors themselves with compositional graph structure that favors the symbolic reasoner by construction.

justification_quote: Two domains (Clevr-derived and Sketch) with 10 continual tasks each - but both benchmarks are self-designed compositional visual classification; no standard CL benchmark or other task family is tested.

Abstract's claim ('demonstrate that NeSyBiCL is effective and leads to superior performance compared to continual learning methods that merely rely on neural architectures') matches the Sec 5 comparisons; the abstract does not state that the two benchmarks are the authors' own design, a mild scope omission.

The biological premise is citation-based: 'Cortical planning interacts with cerebellar prediction and correction, while spinal circuits integrate descending commands with local feedback [8, 11, 44]' (Sec 1) - no own biological evidence; the authors state they 'adopt these functional principles without assuming a one-to-one correspondence'.
note: Cerebellar prediction/correction literature (e.g. Wolpert; Ito) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: The tri-level mapping is functional and instantiated: cortical vision-language planner, recurrent cerebellar modulator integrating proprioception at 200 Hz, and a stateful spiking spinal controller on FPGA whose persistent state is tested by temporal ablation ('multi-step spiking dynamics improve task success over a single-step variant', Fig. 5) and a no-cerebellum baseline (Sec 2.4-2.5).
note: Correspondence is functional, not anatomical - explicitly disclaimed by the authors.

justification_quote: Controlled evidence: cerebellar modulation vs baseline policy reduces mean commanded jerk 75.6% with acceleration traces (Fig. 4); collision stress test on physical hardware gives 54.8% recovery vs 0.0% for evaluated VLA baselines; higher success than OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, UniVLA and WorldVLA across physical tasks (Sec 2.6); hardware measurements for the spinal controller (2.19 ms, 0.87 mJ).
Simulated (LIBERO) and physical bimanual-humanoid deployment across pouring, shaking, precision and recovery tasks - breadth of tasks but a single robot platform and domain (manipulation).

Abstract's quantitative claims (75.6% jerk reduction, 54.8% vs 0.0% recovery, 2.19 ms / 0.87 mJ / 0.4 W FPGA spinal controller) each match Sec 2.4-2.6; the abstract correctly attributes the hardware figures to the spinal controller, and the body notes those measurements exclude the cortical/cerebellar tiers.

The decision-making premise is citation-based: 'the brain often solves decision-making with an evidence accumulation mechanism that may trade time for accuracy... well described by the Drift-Diffusion Model (DDM)' (Abstract, Sec 1, Fig. 2) - no own biological evidence.
note: Canonical evidence-accumulation literature (Ratcliff 1978; Gold & Shadlen 2007 Annu Rev Neurosci) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: The instantiation is direct and verified: test-phase dropout yields stochastic predictions treated as noisy evidence, accumulated to a decision threshold A=0.99 (Sec 3); Fig. 3 plots accuracy vs response time (the speed-accuracy tradeoff that defines the DDM mechanism), and the notation separates dropout-only classifiers (ha,b) from DDDM (Ha,b) so the accumulation component is isolated.

Controlled comparisons across attacks and modalities: 'the DDDM improves the robustness' vs the undefended baseline h0,0 and vs dropout-only ha,b (isolating the DDM accumulation) under 4 white-box and 4 black-box attacks on MNIST (Sec 4.1.1), with the same design on CIFAR10, SpeechCommands and IMDB (Sec 4).
note: Comparisons are against native counterparts and dropout variants, not against adversarial training (discussed qualitatively, Sec 5).

justification_quote: Gains are shown across three task families (image: MNIST/CIFAR10; audio: SpeechCommands; text: IMDB) supporting the 'task-agnostic' claim - each in a single setting with one network per task; no scale or dataset-size variation.

Abstract's claims match the experiments: 'tested in image, speech, and text classification tasks all significantly outperform their native counterparts' (Sec 4, Tables 1-4) and 'task-agnostic defense' backed by the three-modality coverage.

Survey item: 'We provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on memory-augmented GNNs... through the lens of psychology and neuroscience' (Abstract); the multiple-memory-systems framing is synthesis of cited theories (Sec II), not own evidence.
note: FLAG: review/survey paper; no own artifact or experiment; all transitions graded as citation-only evidence.

justification_quote: The review classifies third-party memory-augmented GNNs against biological memory taxonomies and proposes comparison criteria, but instantiates and verifies no correspondence itself.

No experiments are run; performance claims about memory augmentation are assembled from the reviewed papers, and the review provides 'critical discussions on the limitations of these works' rather than controlled comparisons.
No cross-task or cross-scale evaluation; the paper maps the field's landscape, challenges and future directions.

The abstract's claims are review-scoped ('comprehensive review', 'propose a taxonomy... and a set of criteria', 'critical discussions on the limitations') and the paper delivers exactly that; no experimental improvement is claimed.

The hemispheric premise is folk-neuroscience with weak citations: 'Thinking and learning happens in the right hemisphere, and the left hemisphere processes learned information' (Sec 1), motivated by [8] (a slideplayer.com slide, footnote 2) and a DTI concept [6]; no own biological evidence and the stated lateralization division is not established neuroscience.

Mapping is asserted by design naming: right-hemisphere module implements Hopfield associative memory over usage patterns, left-hemisphere Reducer 'analogous to the Wernicke and Broca regions' (Conclusion); the artifact (MapReduce + HDFS + deep Hopfield network) is implemented and run on generated patterns, but the brain correspondence is by assertion.

Results section reports beta/gamma dynamics on generated usage patterns ('At instance alpha1, increasing the value of i... we observe that the values of both beta and gamma increase gradually thus diminishing the recovery accuracy'), with i=1 yielding 100% recovery by construction - suggestive single-setting evidence with no baseline, no real-data accuracy and no comparison.
All experiments use generated (-1,+1) usage patterns; despite the 'Big Data'/Hadoop framing, no scaling measurement, no real datasets and no second task are evaluated.

Abstract claims exceed the evidence: 'improving data disambiguation and overall integration accuracy' and 'scalable... large-scale environments' have no supporting accuracy or scalability measurements in the paper - the only results are beta/gamma pattern-recovery dynamics on synthetic patterns without baselines; the reinforcement/forgetting claim itself does match those dynamics.

The premise is citation-based neuroscience: amodal completion 'essential for human brains to recognize partially occluded images' (citing Muckli 2007; Peters and Kriegeskorte 2021) and ventral/dorsal pathway division (Goodale and Milner 1992; Maunsell and Cook 2002; Ungerleider et al. 2000) (Abstract, Related Work) - no own biological evidence.
note: Dual-stream (Goodale & Milner 1992) and amodal-completion literatures are canonical but were not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: Mapping stated: BIFRNet 'mimics a ventral visual pathway to extract image features and a dorsal visual pathway to distinguish occluded and visible image regions' (VGG16-based VVP, attention-based DVP), plus a knowledge module and a completion module implementing amodal-completion-like inference (Fig. 1, Sec 3); component studies 'show their designated functions' but the pathway correspondence is design analogy.

Tables 2-3: BIFRNet vs VGG16, MaskNet, CoD, TDAPNet and CompNet-Multi across four occlusion levels (0% to 60-80%) and four occluder types on synthetic and real-world datasets, with a Human reference row; 'outperforms the state-of-the-art model by 7% recognition accuracy for highly occluded images'; ablation experiments in the Discussion section cover the components.

Two datasets (synthetic Occluded-Vehicles and real-world Occluded-COCO Vehicles) spanning occlusion levels and types - but a single task (occluded vehicle category recognition, 12 categories); no other domain.

Abstract's claims match the evidence: outperforming existing methods across occlusion levels, 'surpasses other methods by a large margin' for severe occlusion and 'close to the human brain performance' correspond to the Table 2-3 comparisons including the Human row.

Brain premises are citation-based: spatial abstraction via 'a top-down attention computation inspired by conscious reasoning in humans (Dehaene et al., 2020)' (Sec 1.2) and 'Inspired by how the human brain rejects delusional intentions' (Abstract); no own biological evidence, and the delusion-rejection analogy is speculative.
note: Thesis compilation; graded from abstract and contribution chapters.

justification_quote: Mapping stated per contribution: transformer-based top-down attention implements conscious spatial abstraction (Chap. 4), option-based decomposition builds on it (Chap. 5), and 'Inspired by the belief evaluation system in the human brain, we propose a method to reject hallucinated targets by properly learning a target feasibility evaluator' (Chap. 6, Sec 1.2) - implemented, but the brain correspondence is analogy.

Each contribution chapter reports controlled comparisons: Chap. 4 'significantly improves systematic generalization outside the training tasks'; Chap. 5 'Our carefully controlled experiments validate Skipper's significant advantage in zero-shot generalization, compared to some existing state-of-the-art hierarchical planning methods' plus theoretical performance guarantees; Chap. 6 'significant performance improvements in various kinds of planning agents'.

Generalization is the thesis's explicit subject: zero-shot OOD evaluation across distribution-shift gradients (e.g. RDS delta in {0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55}, Sec 2) in all three contribution chapters - but within gridworld-style RL benchmarks; no other domain.

Abstract's claims match the chapter evidence: each framework's improvement claim (systematic generalization, robustness to distributional shifts, delusion mitigation) is attached to its own experimental chapter, and future aspirations are labeled as future research directions.

Survey item: 'this survey adopts a rigorous system-level hardware-software co-design perspective to examine the 2020-2025 trajectory' (Abstract); the biological-plausibility premises (event-driven spiking dynamics, SNN energy promise) are citation-based synthesis.
note: FLAG: review/survey paper; no own artifact or experiment; all transitions graded as citation-only evidence.

justification_quote: The survey dissects how SNNs are mapped onto hardware substrates (quantization, hybrid architectures, toolchains) across third-party works, but instantiates no correspondence itself.

The 'Deployment Paradox' claim (theoretical energy gains 'frequently negated by the inefficiencies of mapping... onto traditional von Neumann substrates') is a synthesis of cited deployments; no controlled comparison is run in this paper.
No cross-task or cross-scale evaluation; the paper maps the 2020-2025 landscape and proposes a roadmap (Neuromorphic OS, Green Cognitive Substrate).
The abstract's claims are review-scoped (critically dissect training complexity, memory wall, software gap; envision a roadmap), which the survey delivers; no experimental improvement is claimed.

The multiscale mechanisms (multi-compartment neurons, synaptic modalities, microcircuits, cortical columns, brain regions, facilitation/FFI/STP/STD, 'what'/'where' pathways [28],[33]) are presented as 'grounded in solid neuroscience' via citation (Abstract, Sec II-III); no own biological evidence.
note: Canonical supports (e.g. Goodale & Milner 1992 dual-stream; short-term plasticity literature) not verified this session, so external grade stays E0.

justification_quote: The artifact instantiates the multiscale emulation and runs: a model with '13 brain regions, approximately 3.7 million neurons, and about 56 million compartments' simulating saccadic movements on MNIST (Sec III), with qualitative feature-extraction and saccade results (Fig. 9); but the brain correspondence is by construction and naming, verified only qualitatively.
note: The model has no learning mechanism - 'all synapses in the neural network are stable synapses'.

justification_quote: Validation is a single demonstration without controls: 'The model's algorithmic efficacy was validated through testing with the observation of handwritten digit images' (Abstract, Sec III-IV) - feature extraction and saccade dynamics are shown (Figs. 9-10) but no accuracy metric, baseline or comparison is reported.

One demonstration setting (static MNIST observation, grayscale digits); the Limitations section states the model is 'a static neural network based on a set of rule systems' with learning, color images and more mechanisms left to future work (Sec V-B).

The abstract's validation claim is modest and matches the evidence ('algorithmic efficacy was validated through testing with the observation of handwritten digit images'); AGI-level framing is aspiration ('In pursuit of AGI pathway... moving towards the long-term goal'), and the body honestly lists the gaps.
